verdicts.rewritten_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline — legal but entirely unshielded, no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: GayCities (14 Dec 2022, updated 1 Sep 2023): 'Top 10 destinations that celebrate marriage equality in the Caribbean and Latin America' ranks Bonaire at #5 — as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are protected by strict anti-discrimination laws, same-sex couples are warmly welcomed; notes Bonaire uses the US dollar. For this record: travel-facing evidence that the island markets itself as equality-friendly with statutory protection behind it.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (5 Dec 2012): the Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union — Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27) on 4 Dec 2012, two visiting residents. For this record: same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012, and the territory has a track record of performing them for visitors.

Saba Tourism official weddings page: the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony is the Court Room in the Administrative Building; registrar Julieta Woods is documented as flexible with couples' wishes; full destination-wedding infrastructure (caterers, flowers, accommodations). For this record: practical logistics for a couple — civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry.

BBC (11 July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta announced a ban on homosexual acts — homosexuality had never before been outlawed in the socially conservative West African state; part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage/family law. SUPERSEDED: the ban entered into force as criminal-code law on 1 Sep 2025. For this record: the decisive policy-reversal date, later confirmed in force.

Africanews (11 Jul 2024, updated 13 Aug 2024): the junta's council approved a decree for a new Personal and Family Code (CPF) that 'enshrines the ban on homosexuality', per a presidency statement, joining the ~22 of 54 African states disallowing same-sex relations. SUPERSEDED: entered into force 1 Sep 2025. For this record: legislative vehicle and date for the criminalisation.

For this record: the operative criminalisation date and penalties; core current-state evidence.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: LGBTQ Nation (Sep 2025): the junta unanimously passed the law; Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala states prison 'between two and five years as well as fines' for perpetrators of 'homosexual or similar practices', and that foreigners will be DEPORTED under the law; junta rule since Sep 2022. For this record: penalties plus explicit deportation exposure for foreign nationals — directly visitor-relevant.

Erasing 76 Crimes (12 Feb 2025): prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 Feb 2025; five unidentified individuals accused; she was widely known for humanitarian work. For this record: lethal violence against visible trans people continues — case specifics (Rangamati, Feb 2025).

Erasing 76 Crimes (7 Apr 2026) citing JMBF's annual report: 260 documented human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals nationwide in 2025 — 'a sharp increase' continuing an upward trend since 2022 — including murder/attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. For this record: the current national incident baseline — magnitude and trend for a visitor assessing exposure.

Global Press Journal: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground; Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013 (a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021), but trans lives have been upended — the featured subject now lives in hiding. For this record: the 2024 regime-change inflection point where formal rights began rolling back in practice.

Washington Blade (5 Aug 2025): a year after protests forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's ouster (August 2024), Bangladesh's LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. For this record: a dated, post-coup security assessment directly relevant to a visitor's risk calculus.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Bangladesh (September 2023, updated April 2026): Section 377 ambiguity persists — it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within s.377 (ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere calling the provision relevant to 'all genders'). For this record: authoritative statement of the legal ambiguity any visitor's conduct sits inside.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Penal Code 1860 criminalises 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment — rarely enforced but used by police to harass people presumed LGBTIQ; hijra are legally recognised as a third gender since 2014 with gender-marker change allowed; LGBTIQ and hijra pride events have been held. For this record: the legal baseline plus the harassment-not-prosecution enforcement pattern and third-gender recognition.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Oct 2025): after hijras refused police extortion money on 10 Sep 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 Sep police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles in Narayanganj — a traditional livelihood. For this record: extortion-driven police violence against visibly trans people, including disruption of street livelihoods.

Erasing 76 Crimes (22 Apr 2024): five transgender/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, per JMBF. For this record: policing of visibly trans people concentrates at transit hubs — the airport itself is a documented hotspot.

UK Upper Tribunal decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal — Home Office country material records Islamist groups calling to prosecute LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues (citing fact-finding missions and IRB Canada). For this record: asylum-grade evidence of state-tolerated hostility; international-regime (asylum) source in scope by design.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: DW (Sep 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued an opinion that EU law as interpreted precludes national legislation like Bulgaria's refusing a trans person ID documents matching presented gender — the court concurred with the AG's proposed reasoning. For this record: EU-law pressure to overturn Bulgaria's legal-recognition ban — dated Sep 2025, pending full judgment.

Strasbourg Observers (17 Dec 2024) on Y.T. v Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition, and the Court made clear those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 registry revision (consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria); Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. For this record: the legal explanation for Bulgaria's recognition ban and its continuing unlawfulness.

Amnesty International (Feb 2015, 'Missing the point'): authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes — legislation exists but bias attacks (spiking in 2013 per the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee) go unpursued; Sofia Prosecution opened some cases. For this record: institutional non-response to bias crime — dated but establishes the pattern later reports inherit.

Human Rights Watch (5 Jun 2017): urges authorities to protect the 10 June Sofia Pride march, noting a group called the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage'. For this record: organised far-right hostility to visible LGBT events — dated evidence of the threat environment around public LGBT visibility.

Novinite (June 2011): the 4th annual Sofia Pride parade passed without incidents under heavy police guard, drawing only a 'Family NGO' protest — after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. For this record: historical baseline of pride security dynamics (protection-dependent order).

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Bahrain' (continuously updated): legal status 'decriminalised since 1976' per ILGA-sourced infobox, with recognition limits and no SOGIESC discrimination protections. For this record: tertiary overview consistent with the Outright/State Department baseline — orientation source only, not stand-alone evidence.

Cairo 52 (7 Feb 2024): in a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia — including refusal of a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. For this record: the documented judicial-refusal practice blocking legal transition at first instance.

Cairo 52 country review: Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade — including UN human-rights bodies and Amnesty International — so local media often serve as the only source. For this record: an evidence-reliability caveat — most findings for this jurisdiction rest on thin, partly remote sourcing.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era law, and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy — but authorities still use 'indecency' and 'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people (the Feb 2024 Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation). For this record: decriminalisation with the residual-arrest pattern — the nuance a visitor's safety turns on.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada RIO BHR105575.E (Aug 2016, covering 2011–Jul 2016): reports that 'according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain' (citing Canada 14 Jul 2016 and Gulf News 5 Feb 2011) plus societal-attitude and treatment-by-authorities research. For this record: a SOURCE CONFLICT — this contradicts the 1976-decriminalisation reading of Wikipedia/Outright/2023 US State Dept; treat as unresolved, flagged for intake follow-up rather than ground truth.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: The Tribune (27 Apr 2016): Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign; BTIU stressed there are no laws protecting transgender and intersex Bahamians, and member Torri Culmer advocates against job termination for trans/intersex workers. For this record: documented absence of trans-specific legal protection plus organised advocacy.

GayLawNet Bahamas law page: on 16 May 1991 consensual same-sex sex was decriminalised (Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act), and in May 1998 the National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced the military, prison service and police do not discriminate. For this record: the statutory decriminalisation date plus an official non-discrimination statement.

The Tribune (8 May 2017): Adrian Brown, 24 (Jamaica-born, US-resident), was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being 'targeted and beat up' because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early Saturday, and wants charges laid. For this record: violent targeting of a gay VISITOR during a major tourist event — direct visitor-risk evidence, dated 2017.

Sarajevo Open Centre, Pink Report 2024 (13 Jun 2024): annual report on LGBTI human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina — the past year saw a number of negative events with significant impact, and the long-visible worsening trend is 'becoming increasingly evident'. For this record: current national climate assessment from the leading local monitor.

Balkan Diskurs (25 Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice — the Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions document changes on 'completed' medical transition, constraints described as discriminatory and degrading. For this record: the documentation pathway a trans person navigating the system faces — resident-facing, not a border issue.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Human Rights Watch (4 Feb 2014): violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers — Sarajevo Open Centre staff said they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier; HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of attackers. For this record: precedent that organised anti-LGBT violence occurs even WITH prior police coordination (dated 2014, context for later attacks).

GlobalGayz (2012): same-sex conduct decriminalised in the Federation of BiH (1996) and Republika Srpska (1998) via the two entities' own criminal codes; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation but omitted gender identity as originally intended. For this record: entity-level legal baseline plus the pre-2016 gender-identity protection gap.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): BiH's amended Anti-Discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity with correct local terminology — SOC co-presented the amendments with the Agency for Gender Equality after fall-2015 public consultations. For this record: the statutory protection now on the books at state level.

Sarajevo Open Centre (Jul 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation explicitly naming sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances — SOC coordinator Vladana Vasić confirming the long-sought coalition win. For this record: entity-level sentencing enhancement for bias attacks in FBiH (RS runs its own separate regime).

verdicts.rewritten_summary: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: South Carolina is called out for expanding its bathroom ban to universities (campus settings added to the pre-existing restriction); the assessment's rubric ranks states on adult and youth law severity by reading bills, and South Carolina's expansion places it among the escalating states rather than the harshest tier.

ACLU of South Carolina (May 18, 2026): Governor Henry McMaster signed House Bill 4756 into law on Friday May 15, 2026, requiring transgender students in South Carolina public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth; ACLU frames it as discrimination against trans students in K-12 and higher education and notes the Senate amended the bill before passage. Press release dated May 18, 2026.

ACLU Florida know-your-rights on the 2023 restroom law (Fla. Stat. 553.865): refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can be criminal trespass, but the law only applies in buildings owned or leased by the state or local government — state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons/jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private. Private businesses are outside its scope; the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

NBC News (2025): Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after declaring 'I am here to break the law' and entering a women's restroom — believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. She faces a misdemeanor trespass charge punishable by up to 60 days in jail; at least 14 states have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Metro Weekly (July 6, 2025): on June 20, 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw out the trespass case against Marcy Rheintgen on a legal technicality — as a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate — so the statute was never substantively tested. She had been charged March 19, 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Statehouse.

Equality Florida travel advisory (April 12, 2023): the organization took the 'unprecedented step' of warning about risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people, reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks, and book bans/curriculum censorship. The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; EQFL reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

National law-vs-violence analysis (2008-2025 data): Florida scores 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year, labelled 'Do Not Travel'; the article's core finding is that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates (trendline nearly flat across the 26 states with data) — legal climate and street-level violence are independent visitor risks.

July 2026 national risk assessment: Nebraska's governor has issued an executive order ending legal recognition of transgender people; the assessment places Nebraska in a mid-tier group whose laws 'haven't reached the same level of severity as the worst states', with further restrictive bills proposed in the current cycle. Rankings derive from an expert rubric reading of bills (thousands reviewed).

National law-vs-violence analysis (2008-2025 data): North Carolina appears in the dataset with trans-women murder rates in the ~3.0-6.4 per 100k range across the article's views (12 recorded deaths), used to argue that state law grades do not predict killings — the chart places North Carolina's law climate in the safer grades alongside moderate recorded violence. For visitors: legal climate is a poor proxy for street-level violence exposure.

July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: Montana is flagged as a special case — it has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but those laws have been repeatedly blocked or enjoined under the state constitution, improving its standing on the assessment's rubric (which ranks states by expert reading of bills on adult and youth restrictions).

National risk assessment update: Montana is the single state that improves in the 2026 rankings, because the state court system has repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans laws under the state constitution; adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. Youth-side picture remains unstable nationally (federal policy shifts and litigation).

PBS NewsHour (Aug 29, 2023): Missouri's ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors took effect after a judge denied an emergency request from civil-rights advocates to halt it. The SAFE Act bars hormones, puberty blockers and transition surgeries for minors unless treatment began before Aug 28, 2023, and is set to expire in 2027 as negotiated with Senate Democrats; ACLU of Missouri said litigation would continue.

July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: Missouri prohibits gender-affirming care for both incarcerated adults and transgender youth and has seen new restrictive laws proposed in the current cycle, placing it below the harshest tier but on an worsening trajectory per the assessment's bill-reading rubric.
